Index

A dictionary of the tools and terms used across this dashboard.

Every control, marker and convention in this dashboard, grouped by where you meet it. If you are looking for what the catalog is and how it was compiled, that is the Info tab.

No terms match that filter.

Getting Started

The four tabs, and what each is for.

Map tab

The main view: every figure in the catalog placed where they were born, studied and died. Panels on the left narrow what is shown (by date, by attribute); panels on the right control how it is drawn and let you find one person.

Nothing is shown until it is selected: with no filters applied, every mapped figure is included.

Data tab

The same catalog as a sortable, filterable table, plus a chart builder. Use it when you want to read the underlying records rather than look at geography.

The Map and Data tabs share their category filters: add a filter in either and it appears in the other. Their date filters are separate, because the Map filters on a timeline and the table filters on a year column.

Index tab

This page: every control, marker and convention in the dashboard, grouped by where you meet it. Use the filter box to jump straight to a term — it searches the descriptions, not just the headings.

It covers how the dashboard works. For what the catalog is and how it was compiled, see the Info tab.

Info tab

The project itself: what the catalog is, where it came from, how to cite it, and how it was compiled.

Copy link

Copies a URL that reopens the exact view you are looking at: the year window, the active filters, the map position, the selected person, which layers are on, and which tab.

The address bar already tracks this as you work, so you can also just copy it. The button exists because that URL is easy to miss, and invisible on mobile.

A link identifies a person by name, so it keeps pointing at the right person after the catalog is updated. If a figure or a filter value is later removed, that part of the link is quietly ignored rather than guessed at.

Feedback

Opens a form for reporting an error or suggesting a change.

BETA

This dashboard is under active development. Records are still being checked, and both the data and the interface may change.

Layers

Right-hand panel. Controls what is drawn on the map.

Birth Clusters

Green markers at each place of birth. On by default.

Education Institutions

Orange markers at each place of study. One marker per institution, not per student: a university attended by fifty people is a single dot labelled 50.

Death Clusters

Red markers at each place of death.

Life Vectors

A grey line tracing each figure’s path: birthplace → each place of education in the order attended → place of death. Someone with no recorded death place still has a line if they studied somewhere; someone with neither has no line, since a single point is not a path.

Birth Heatmap / Education Heatmap / Death Heatmap

Density shading rather than individual markers — useful for seeing where activity concentrated without counting dots. Fades out as you zoom in past the point where individual markers are readable.

Heatmaps are drawn from the true recorded coordinates, not the slightly-separated marker positions (see Marker separation), so they show real density.

The education heatmap counts people, not institutions: a university with fifty students burns fifty times brighter than one with a single student, even though both are one dot on the Education Institutions layer.

Basemap — Place Labels

The underlying map’s own text: country, region, city and water names. Turn off for an uncluttered map when the labels compete with the markers.

Does not affect the marker counts, which are ours, not the basemap’s.

Basemap — Borders

Administrative boundary lines: country, state, county and city. These are period borders — they change with the year shown (see Historical basemap).

Independent of Place Labels: country names are labels, country outlines are borders. You can have either without the other.

Cluster

When markers are too close together to read, they merge into one circle showing how many are inside. Click a cluster to zoom in and break it apart. Clusters dissolve into individual markers by zoom level 10.

An education cluster counts people, not institutions, so it means the same thing as a birth or death cluster.

Marker separation

Markers at identical coordinates would sit exactly on top of each other, making all but the top one unclickable. Three things prevent that: busy places (more than five figures) are fanned onto a small ring; everything else is nudged by about 100 m; and where one person was born and died in the same place, the two markers are pushed a few hundred metres apart in opposite directions.

So a marker’s position is accurate to the place, not the street. The heatmaps and the Data tab use the true coordinates.

Temporal Controller

Left-hand panel, top. Restricts the map to a period, and animates through it.

Filter by Timeline

Turns the date filter on. While off, every figure is shown regardless of date and the readout says All years.

Min / Max

The two ends of the year window. Drag either handle; they cannot cross.

Alive in range

What the timeline actually selects. A figure is included when their lifetime overlaps the window — not when they were born inside it. Someone born 1590 and died 1660 appears in a 1600–1650 window, because they were alive throughout it.

Where only one year is recorded, that year must fall inside the window. Where neither is recorded, the figure is excluded whenever the timeline is on — an undated person cannot be shown to be alive at any particular time.

Playback

Reveals the Play controls, which sweep a single year forward through the timeline so you can watch activity move across the map.

Play / Pause

Starts and stops the sweep. Play from a paused position resumes; play from the end starts over. Pausing leaves the map exactly on the year shown.

Speed

0.25x to 2.00x, plus 5.00x. One year per step; the speed sets how fast the steps run.

Current Year

The year, or year range, the map is currently showing. During playback this is a single year; when you set a window by hand it shows both ends.

Advanced Query Builder

Left-hand panel. Filters the map by any recorded attribute.

Category dropdowns

One per filterable field — discipline, instrument, society, institution, degree, means of support, patronage, gender, religion, family wealth, father’s occupation, country of birth, country of death. Choosing a value adds it to Active Filters.

Active Filters

The filters currently applied, as removable chips. Click the × on a chip to drop that filter.

These chips are shared with the Data tab: add one here and it appears there too, and vice versa.

Match: ALL (AND)

A figure must satisfy every active filter. Narrows as you add filters. This is the default.

Astronomy AND Jesuit → only Jesuit astronomers.

Match: ANY (OR)

A figure needs satisfy only one active filter. Widens as you add filters.

Astronomy OR Jesuit → every astronomer, plus every Jesuit.

Apply Query

Redraws the map against the current filters. Adding or removing a chip already redraws, so this is mostly a way to force a refresh.

Clear

Removes every active filter. Does not touch the timeline or the layers.

Export selection (CSV)

Downloads the currently selected figures as a spreadsheet — whatever survives the timeline and the filters — with their coordinates, dates and every catalogued attribute.

The filename records the year window and the head count, so exports stay distinguishable from one another.

Finding and Reading a Person

Right-hand panel, and what happens when you click.

Find a Person

Type any part of a name. Choosing a suggestion selects that figure: the map frames their whole life path and opens their record.

Searches alternate names as well as the catalogued one, so a figure is findable by the name you know rather than the one the compiler filed them under. Typing Abelard finds Pierre Abailard; Albatenius finds al-Battānī. Where a match came from an alternate name, the suggestion says which one, so an unexpected result explains itself.

Suggestions show a birth year to separate figures who share a name. A match on the catalogued name is listed before a match on an alternate one.

Only figures with a mapped birthplace appear here. Anyone whose coordinates were never recorded has no marker to select — use the Data tab, which lists every catalogued figure whether or not they can be placed.

Selection highlight

The selected figure is drawn in purple, with a dashed line along their path, on top of everything else. It stays visible while you pan, filter, or run playback.

Clear selection

Drops the highlight and closes the record. Appears only while someone is selected.

Person record

The panel that opens when you click a marker. Lists what the catalog holds: alternate names, birth and death (place and year), gender, education, father, disciplines, societies, religion, means of support, patronage, instruments, and the sources the entry was compiled from.

Fields with nothing recorded are left out rather than shown empty, so the record shows what is known.

Life vector tooltip

Hovering a life vector names the figure and the chain of places their line passes through, in order. Consecutive repeats collapse, so someone born and educated in the same city reads Paris → Padua, not Paris → Paris → Padua.

Synchronised hover

Hovering any one of a figure’s markers highlights all of them at once — birth, education stops, death, and the line joining them — so you can see a whole life without clicking. Only layers that are switched on light up.

Legend

Bottom right. Hover any entry for a fuller description of what the colour means.

Education

What the orange markers hold.

Education bubble

One marker per institution, sized and labelled by how many of the currently selected figures studied there. Change the filters and the numbers change with them.

A dot with a single student is drawn small and unlabelled — a "1" on every lone marker would be noise.

Grouped by institution

Bubbles group by institution name, not by coordinate. One geocode often covers many separate schools — twenty-one distinct institutions share the centre of Paris — and grouping by position would merge them into a single meaningless dot. Institutions sharing a point are fanned onto a small ring so each stays separately clickable.

Not Specified

A bubble pooling everyone recorded as having studied in a city whose institution the source never names. It sits alongside that city’s named institutions and carries a note saying so.

It is not a school, and not a spelling variant of one. Paris, for example, has twenty-one named institutions plus one Not Specified bubble.

Roster

Everyone who studied at that institution under the current filters, with the years they were there, earliest first. Undated figures fall to the bottom.

View timeline

Opens a chart of who was at an institution when — one bar per stay, drawn against a shared year axis, so overlapping figures line up vertically. This is how you spot who might plausibly have met.

Click any row to find that person on the map. Close with ×, by clicking outside, or with Esc. The button appears only when at least one figure there has a recorded year.

Open-ended bar

On the timeline, a bar that fades out at one end means the source records only one of the two years. The fade marks where knowledge stops — it is not an estimate of when they left.

Figures with no years at all are not plotted; they are listed under the axis, so they are visible without inventing a position for them.

Recorded stays

The timeline subtitle may report more stays than people. That is not an error: someone can have two spells at one institution. Aquinas was at Paris twice.

The Map Itself

The historical basemap under the data.

Historical basemap

The underlying map is OpenHistoricalMap, in which places and boundaries carry start and end dates. It is filtered to whatever year the Temporal Controller shows, so borders, place names and settlements are those of the period — not modern ones.

With a range selected, the basemap shows the world as of the end of the window. With the timeline off, it shows the latest year in the catalog.

Coverage is contributed by volunteers and is uneven: sparse coverage means missing borders in some periods, not a mistake in the catalog.

Place names in English

Basemap labels use the English name where OpenHistoricalMap records one, and fall back to the local name where it does not — which, for many historical places, is the only name there is.

Infrastructure

Roads, railways, airports and buildings are removed from the basemap. They are modern, and irrelevant to where a 16th-century scholar studied.

Attribution

Bottom right. Credits OpenHistoricalMap’s contributors, whose data is licensed ODbL. Required by that licence — please leave it in place.

Scale bar

Under the legend. Shows the distance a screen length represents at the current zoom.

Opening view

The map opens on the whole world. The catalog reaches from San Francisco to Japan, and opening on Europe would hide an eighth of it behind a pan you had no reason to make — even though most of the figures are European.

The exact zoom is fitted to your window rather than fixed, since the zoom that shows the world on a desktop shows only a region on a phone.

Zoom

Bottom right, or scroll / pinch. The map draws a single world rather than repeating east–west, so a life vector never wraps around the back of the globe.

Data Explorer

The Data tab: the catalog as a table.

Search all columns

Free text across every column at once — including Also Known As, so alternate names are searchable here too. Matches anywhere, not just at the start of a word.

Also Known As

A column listing a figure’s alternate names. Unlike the Map’s search box, the table covers every catalogued figure, including those with no coordinates who never appear on the map.

Year range

Pick Born year or Died year, then a minimum and/or maximum. Either end can be left blank for an open bound.

This is a plain column filter and behaves differently from the Map’s timeline, which asks whether someone was alive during a window.

Match ALL / ANY

As in the Query Builder: ALL requires every chip, ANY requires only one. Shared with the Map.

Add filter: category

Pick a category, then a value, to add a filter chip. The same chips as the Map’s Active Filters.

Clear

Drops every filter chip, the search text, and the year range. Table only.

Export filtered (CSV)

Downloads exactly the rows currently shown, with every column. The filename records the row count.

Years export as raw numbers, so BC years appear as negatives (–384, not "384 BC"). That keeps the file sortable and computable in a spreadsheet.

Hide charts

Collapses the chart panel to give the table the full width.

Column sorting

Click any column heading to sort; click again to reverse. Blanks always sort last, in either direction, so an empty cell never displaces a real value from the top.

Reordering columns

Drag a column heading sideways to move it; it drops in before the heading you release on. A grip appears on the left of each heading on hover.

The new order carries through everything the table drives — the rows, the record detail, and the CSV export all follow it — and survives filtering and sorting. Dragging and click-to-sort share the same heading and do not interfere: a drag reorders, a click sorts.

The order is not saved between visits; a reload restores the default.

Summary strip

Above the table: how many figures are in view, the span of their birth years, and the three commonest disciplines among them. Updates with every filter.

Row detail

Click any row for the full record, including long note fields the table truncates.

Show on map

In the row detail: jumps to the Map tab and selects that figure. Disabled when a record has no birth coordinates, since there is no marker to show.

Data-quality badge

At the top of each row detail: how many of the compiled sources disagreed about this figure, and on which fields. Green for none, amber for one or two, red beyond that.

It measures source agreement, not correctness: sources can agree and still be wrong. Treat a red badge as a prompt to check the primary sources yourself.

Chart Builder

Data tab, right-hand panel. Charts whatever the table currently shows.

What gets charted

Always the filtered rows, never the whole catalog. The chart’s subtitle records which filters were active and how many figures they matched, so a chart exported to PNG still says what it is a chart of.

Type

Bar — compare categories. Line / Area — change over time. Pie / Doughnut — shares of a whole. Histogram — the distribution of one number. Scatter — two numbers against each other.

The controls below change with the type: only the ones that apply are shown.

Group by

What forms the categories, or the x-axis. Pick a text field (discipline, country) or a number (born year).

Bin size

When grouping by a number, how wide each bucket is. 10 gives decades, 100 gives centuries.

Split by

Breaks each bar or line into sub-series by a second field — disciplines by decade, split by religion. Limited to the eight commonest values.

Measure / of field

What the height means: Count of figures (the default), or the Average, Median, Sum, Min or Max of a chosen numeric field — average lifespan by country, for instance.

Y axis / Color by

Scatter only: the second number to plot, and an optional field to colour the points by.

Sort

Value ↓ or Value ↑ orders the categories by size; Label A–Z orders them alphabetically.

Numeric groupings always run in numeric order regardless, since a chronology out of order is not a chronology.

Exclude Unknown

Drops Unknown from the chart’s categories. The catalog records Unknown as an answer rather than leaving a blank, so it charts as a category like any other — and it is often the biggest one: religion is Unknown for 228 of 366 figures, father’s wealth for 270.

Also drops Not Specified, which is what the sources say when an institution was not recorded.

Off by default: the catalog says Unknown, and hiding that unasked would overstate how much is known. When it is on, the chart’s subtitle says so — an exported PNG travels without this panel, so it has to carry the caveat itself.

What is excluded is the value, not the figure: someone recorded as "Astronomy; Unknown" still counts under Astronomy. Numeric axes are unaffected, since a missing number is blank rather than "Unknown".

Max groups / Remainder as “Other”

Caps how many categories are drawn, so a long tail does not crush the chart. Note this is unrelated to Exclude Unknown: “Other” is a bucket this control creates, not a value the sources recorded.

Tick Remainder as “Other” to roll everything past the cap into one bar rather than drop it silently.

Bins

Histogram only: how many buckets to divide the range into.

Horizontal / Stacked

Bar charts: turn sideways when category names are long; stack a split series to read totals rather than compare parts.

Build chart / PNG

Draws the chart, and downloads it as an image. The PNG carries the title and filter summary with it.

Conventions and Caveats

How to read what the dashboard shows — and what it does not claim.

BC years

Displayed as 384 BC everywhere a reader sees them. AD years are shown plainly, with no era suffix, since the catalog is overwhelmingly post-classical and the suffix would be noise on almost every row.

Underneath, a BC year is stored as a negative number, which is why timelines, sorting and lifespan arithmetic work across year zero. CSV exports keep the negative form.

Unknown

The catalog records Unknown as a value in its own right. Treated as "nothing recorded" and left out of the display rather than shown as the word "Unknown".

????

In an education roster or timeline: this year is not recorded. Shown rather than hidden, so a missing year is visibly missing instead of silently absent.

Alternate names

The Latin, Arabic and vernacular forms a figure is also known by — Peter Abelard for Pierre Abailard, Savasorda for Abraham Bar Ḥiyya, Albertus Magnus for Albert the Great. About half the catalog carries at least one.

They are searchable on both tabs, and listed in a figure’s record under Also known as. The Data tab shows them in its own column.

Which form is treated as the main name is the compiler’s choice, not a judgement about which is correct.

Names

Shown as a reader would say them. Where the source splits a name awkwardly, the display corrects it: Albert of Saxony, not "of Saxony Albert"; Aristotle, not "Aristotle Aristotle".

The Data tab files names by surname for sorting — Galilei, Galileo — but an epithet takes no comma, since "of Saxony" is not a first name.

Lifespan

Died year minus born year. A count of years, not a date, so it is never labelled BC.

One record, several people

A few entries cover more than one person — the Banū Mūsā record is three brothers. They map as a single point.

Absence is not evidence

An empty region may mean nobody worked there, or that Westfall’s catalog does not cover it. The catalog is a compilation with its own scope and biases, and the map inherits every one of them. See the Info tab.

Keyboard

Esc closes the education timeline, the record detail, and the search suggestions. Enter in the person search picks the first match.

Filter this index

The box at the top of this page hides any entry that does not match what you type. It searches the descriptions, not just the headings.
